title: Friuli Venezia Giulia
quiz.0.question: Which is Friuli’s finest appellation?
quiz.0.explanation: Collio’s whites are considered the finest in Friuli and among the best in Italy; by vineyard area and production it is Friuli’s third-largest DOC.
quiz.1.question: DNA research has shown Friulano (formerly Tocai Friulano) to be identical to which grape?
quiz.1.explanation: DNA research has proven Friulano to be the same variety as Sauvignonasse, native to the Gironde; it is regarded as Friuli’s “traditional” white grape and is its third most planted variety.
quiz.2.question: How is orange wine made?
quiz.2.options.1: White grapes made with red-wine techniques (skin contact)
quiz.2.explanation: Inspired by Gravner and Radikon, some producers make white wine using red-wine techniques — long skin-contact fermentation and long ageing in large neutral oak — with Gravner also introducing amphorae; the wines are deep gold, somewhat oxidative and phenolic.
quiz.3.question: What do locals call the sandstone and calcareous marl soils of Friuli’s eastern hills?
quiz.3.explanation: The sandstone and calcareous marl of the eastern hills is called ponca locally; in Collio it is known geologically as Flysch di Cormons.
slides.0.title: 🌿 Friuli Venezia Giulia
slides.0.subtitle: The birthplace of modern Italian white wine
slides.1.title: 🗺️ A Wine Treasure on the North-East Border
slides.1.content:
Friuli Venezia Giulia (Friuli for short) is a small autonomous region in Italy’s north-east corner, wedged between Austria, Slovenia and the Italian mainland — a meeting point of Italian, Germanic and Slavic cultures. It is recognised as the birthplace of modern Italian white winemaking.

70%+of plantings are white grapes (and rising)
<30%of plantings are red grapes (growing in importance)
40%+of production is DOC

🌍 Geography

  • Location: Italy’s north-east corner, bordering Austria to the north and Slovenia to the east
  • Landscape: the Alps (no wine), the eastern hills, the central plain and the lower coastal plain
  • Soils: ponca (sandstone and calcareous marl) in the eastern hills, alluvial soils and gravel on the plains, limestone in the Carso
  • Size: about 23,000 ha, mostly small to medium family estates, with cooperatives playing a small role
slides.2.title: 🗺️ Friuli Venezia Giulia DOCG & DOC Interactive Map
slides.3.title: 🏛️ History and Cultural Heritage
slides.3.content:
From pre-Roman vineyards to the white wine revolution of the 1960s, Friuli reshaped Italian white wine.

📜

Antiquity

◆ Collio’s vineyards date back before Roman times, and were already famous then

◆ Picolit has been grown in Friuli since Roman times

⛪

Middle Ages

◆ Ribolla Gialla, Schioppettino and Malvasia Istriana are documented since at least the 13th century

◆ The Abbey of Rosazzo, founded in the late 10th century, whose monks did much to develop local viticulture and winemaking

👑

Austrian rule and international grapes

◆ In the 15th century, under Austrian rule, Riesling, Müller Thurgau, Welschriesling and Blaufränkisch arrived

◆ In the 19th century (before phylloxera) came Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot and Cabernet Franc

🇮🇹

Joining Italy

◆ The Colli Orientali area joined Italy in the second half of the 19th century

◆ Collio only joined after World War I

◆ After World War II the border was redrawn and some Collio vineyards ended up in Slovenia, though producers may still label that fruit Collio DOC

🌟

The white wine revolution (from the late 1960s)

◆ Mario Schiopetto, inspired by German winemaking, introduced temperature-controlled fermentation, stainless steel, refrigeration, pneumatic presses and sterile bottling to prevent any oxidation

◆ Livio Felluga and others followed; from the 1970s attention also turned to the vineyard

◆ The key to success: single-varietal bottling, with native and international grapes alike

🧡

Two new paths

◆ Super-whites: in the late 1970s Jermann released Vintage Tunina, pioneering top white blends of native and international grapes

◆ Orange wine: in Collio, Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon made white wine with red-wine techniques, and Gravner introduced amphorae

🌐 Cultural standing and influence

🏆 Birthplace of modern white wine

The clean, fresh, aromatic, varietally distinct style of white began here

🧡 A home of orange wine

Gravner and Radikon in Collio drove the long skin-contact style of white wine

🌍 Cross-border terroir

Some Collio vineyards lie in Slovenia; Vitovska, Terrano and Malvasia Istriana are natives shared with Slavic neighbours
slides.4.title: 🍇 The Three Core Appellations
slides.4.content:
Top whites

Collio DOC

Location: Gorizia province, along the Slovenian border between the Judrio and Isonzo rivers

Soils: alternating sandstone and calcareous marl (Flysch di Cormons, i.e. ponca)

Size: Friuli’s third-largest DOC, over 80% white

Style: from pure varietal character to complex, structured wines; top blends are labelled Collio Bianco

Key grapes: Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon, Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Malvasia

💎 Its whites are considered Friuli’s finest and among Italy’s best
Red and white

Friuli Colli Orientali DOC

Location: the eastern hills north of Collio, centred on Cividale

Soils: the same ponca hills as Collio

Size: Friuli’s second-largest DOC

Style: Friulano is the most planted white; reds are best between Buttrio, Cividale and Manzano

DOCGs: Picolit, Ramandolo and Rosazzo all lie within this DOC

🍯 The boundary with Collio is historical rather than climatic or geological
Largest

Friuli Grave DOC

Location: the central plain

Soils: fertile mixed sand, clay and gravel

Character: the largest DOC by area and production

Style: fresh, easy, everyday

Key grapes: Pinot Grigio, Merlot and others

💰 Merlot is very well suited to this gravelly plain
slides.5.title: 🪨 Ponca Soils and Terroir
slides.5.content:
Ponca is the sandstone and calcareous marl of the eastern hills — known geologically in Collio as Flysch di Cormons — and the foundation of Friuli’s top white wines.

🪨 Friuli’s soils

⛰️ The eastern hills

Soils: sandstone and calcareous marl (ponca)

Appellations: Collio, Friuli Colli Orientali

Status: the best land for vines

🌾 The central plain

Soils: fertile mixed sand, clay and gravel

Appellations: Friuli Grave and others

Status: a large production area

🌊 The lower coastal plain

Location: facing the lagoons

Appellations: Friuli Aquileia, Friuli Annia, Friuli Latisana

🪨 The Carso plateau

Soils: iron-rich red sandy clay over limestone

Landscape: hard to farm; vines often grow beside olive trees on small terraces called “pastini”

🍷 The terroir of Collio

FactorIn CollioEffect
LandscapeA series of rounded, south-facing hills (Collio means “hills”)Steep slopes mean hand harvesting
SeaOnly about 30 km from the AdriaticSea breezes moderate temperatures
MountainsCold air descends from the Alps to the northCool nights
SitesSunny, often terraced slopes are called “ronchi” (singular ronco)Often used in estate, vineyard or wine names
Sub-areasCapriva, Oslavia, San Floriano del Collio and othersNot legally recognised and cannot appear on labels

🗺️ Soils of the main appellations

Collio DOC

Soils: ponca (Flysch di Cormons)

Landscape: south-facing hills

Wines: Friuli’s finest whites

Size: third-largest DOC

Friuli Colli Orientali DOC

Soils: ponca hills

Landscape: an extension of the Collio hills

Wines: excellent reds and whites

Size: second-largest DOC

Friuli Grave DOC

Soils: sand, clay, gravel

Landscape: the central plain

Wines: fresh and easy

Size: the largest DOC

Friuli Isonzo DOC

Soils: the plain along the Isonzo

Landscape: south of Collio

Wines: potential to rival the hill appellations

Sub-zones: Rive Alte, Rive di Giare

🌤️ Climate factors

🌊
The Adriatic

Sea breezes moderate temperatures in the hills and plains

⛰️
The Alpine barrier

The Carnic and Julian Alps to the north; descending cold air brings cool nights

❄️
Coolest in the north

Ramandolo, far to the north, is Friuli’s coolest growing area

☀️
Warmer in the south

The southern Colli Orientali (Buttrio, Cividale, Manzano) is warmer and best for reds
slides.6.title: 🌟 Friuli’s Main White Grapes
slides.6.content:
⭐ Friulano

(Tocai Friulano before 2007)

Identity: DNA has shown it to be Sauvignonasse from the Gironde

Status: Friuli’s “traditional” white grape and third most planted (over 8%)

Where: the most planted white in Colli Orientali; the backbone of Rosazzo DOCG

Pinot Grigio

Status: Friuli’s most planted grape (21%)

Style: mostly simple, easy and crisp

The eastern hills also make serious versions in the style of Alsace Pinot Gris: rich, round and full, with floral and nutty notes

Ribolla Gialla

History: grown in the eastern hills since at least the 13th century, traditionally centred on Oslavia in Collio

Revival: it fell below 1% of Friuli DOC production in the 1990s before producers devoted to native grapes revived it

Today one of the region’s most distinctive whites

Malvasia Istriana

Identity: a member of the Malvasia family; its name suggests Istria, but it has been grown in Friuli since the 13th century

Status: dry Malvasia from the eastern hills or the Carso ranks among Italy’s best of its kind

Labels usually just say “Malvasia”

Sauvignon Blanc

Local name: Sauvignon

Status: one of Italy’s most successful regions for Sauvignon Blanc

Eastern-hills versions are crisp and pure, from citrus and grass to peach and tropical fruit

🍯 Picolit

(sweet wine)

History: grown since Roman times; thought to originate around Rosazzo

Trait: very prone to shatter (poor pollination), giving sparse bunches of small, sweet berries and tiny yields

Elegant, complex sweet wines; the star of Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit DOCG
slides.7.title: 🍇 Native and International Grapes in Depth
slides.7.content:
🇮🇹 Native white grapes in detail

⭐ Friulano (Tocai Friulano)

📜 The name

◆ Before 2007: labelled Tocai Friulano

◆ From 2007: the EU upheld a complaint from Hungary’s Tokaji producers, so labels may no longer say “Tocai” and now say Friulano

◆ Grape register: still listed as Tocai Friulano in the national register

◆ Veneto: now called Tai or Tai Bianco

🧬 Identity

Once: thought to be native to Friuli

DNA: the same variety as Sauvignonasse, native to the Gironde

Today: regarded as Friuli’s “traditional” white grape

🗺️ Where

Colli Orientali: the most planted white

Rosazzo DOCG: the backbone of the blend

Collio: among the top three by area

🍋 Ribolla Gialla

📜 An ancient grape

◆ Records: grown in the eastern hills along the Slovenian border since at least the 13th century

◆ Heartland: around the village of Oslavia in Collio

◆ Decline: it faded after phylloxera, falling below 1% of Friuli DOC production in the 1990s

🌟 Revival

Producers devoted to native grapes brought it back, and it is now one of the region’s most distinctive whites

🧡 Orange wine

Gravner and Radikon in Oslavia both make long skin-contact whites from Ribolla Gialla

🌸 Malvasia Istriana

🌍 Origin and identity

◆ Name: suggests the Istrian peninsula (today north-west Croatia)

◆ Records: grown in Friuli since the 13th century

◆ Shared native: like Vitovska and Terrano, a native shared by Friuli and its Slavic neighbours

🍷 Standing

Dry Malvasia from the eastern hills or the Carso plateau is considered among the best of its kind in Italy; labels usually just say “Malvasia”

🍯 Verduzzo Giallo (Ramandolo)

🍷 A sweet-wine grape

◆ Appellation: Ramandolo DOCG, made from 100% Verduzzo Giallo

◆ Local name: Ramandolo

◆ Also: Verduzzo Friulano is one of the signature grapes of Cialla

🍇 Winemaking

Deliberately late-harvested, sometimes into November, once the grapes are overripe or shrivelling on the vine; most producers then dry them further (appassimento)

💎 Picolit

👑 A historic sweet wine

◆ History: grown since Roman times, thought to originate around Rosazzo

◆ Shatter: poor pollination at flowering gives sparse bunches of small, sweet berries

◆ Result: tiny yields

🍷 Revival

It declined in the early 20th century and was rescued by the Perusini family; it regained its fame in the late 1960s and early 1970s and is now rare and expensive

🌐 International grapes in Friuli

Pinot Grigio

Status: the most planted grape (21%)

Style: mostly simple and easy; rich, round serious versions in the eastern hills

Arrived: 19th century

Sauvignon Blanc

Status: one of Italy’s most successful regions for it

Style: crisp and pure, from citrus and grass to peach and tropical fruit

Collio: the second most planted grape

Chardonnay

Share: about 7%

Use: varietal wines and white blends

Rosazzo: allowed as a blending grape

Merlot

Status: the second most planted grape (15%)

Arrived: second half of the 19th century

Terroir: very well suited to the gravelly plains; Friuli is one of Italy’s main Merlot regions

🍷 Native red grapes (under 30% red)

🇮🇹 Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso

Identity: the finest of the Refosco family and Friuli’s traditional signature red; native to the Carso, now grown region-wide

Name: “red stalk”, as the stalks turn red at ripeness

Style: a light, fruity, unoaked version or a rich, ripe, structured one

Oak: helps soften its angular tannins, but should be used with restraint

🇮🇹 Schioppettino (Ribolla Nera)

History: grown since at least the 13th century, near extinction after phylloxera, revived in the 1970s

Flavour: deep colour, intense floral and black fruit aromas with a peppery, spicy core

Structure: powerful and concentrated, with high acidity and tannin

Where: Prepotto, Cialla

🇮🇹 Pignolo and Tazzelenghe

Pignolo: Rosazzo has been known for Pignolo for centuries

Tazzelenghe: a native widely planted in the Colli Orientali before phylloxera

Trend: producers are increasingly turning to these natives

🌐 Merlot and the Cabernets

Share: Merlot 15%, Cabernet Franc 5%, Cabernet Sauvignon 3%

Collio: these three are the main reds, as varietals or blended into Collio Rosso

Colli Orientali: Rosso may blend native and international grapes in any proportion
slides.8.title: 🌍 The Four Landscapes and Planting Statistics (IWS)
slides.8.content:
The four landscapes

Friuli divides broadly into four parts: the Alps (no wine), the eastern hills (The Eastern Hills — the best land for vines, with sandstone and calcareous marl known locally as “ponca”), the central plain (The Central Plain — a large area of fertile sand, clay and gravel) and the lower coastal plain (The Lower Coastal Plain, facing the lagoons). The Carso plateau has iron-rich red sandy clay over limestone; it is hard to farm, so growers use every available slope, often planting vines next to olive trees.

Plantings by grape: Pinot Grigio 21% · Merlot 15% · Friulano 8% · Sauvignon Blanc 7% · Chardonnay 7% · Cabernet Franc 5% · Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso 4% · Cabernet Sauvignon 3% · Others 29%

Where the grapes came from: three waves

19th-century international grapes: Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot and Cabernet Franc all arrived in the 19th century (before phylloxera); after phylloxera, being easier to grow, they gradually displaced the native grapes and today underpin Friuli’s best wines
15th-century Germanic grapes: Riesling, Müller Thurgau, Welschriesling and Blaufränkisch arrived under Austrian rule; they play a minor role today but add to the region’s diversity
Cross-border Slavic natives: along the borders with Slovenia and Croatia, Vitovska (a Carso white), Terrano (a Carso red) and Malvasia Istriana are considered natives shared by Friuli and its Slavic neighbours — the name suggests Istria (today north-west Croatia), but Malvasia Istriana has been documented in Friuli since the 13th century, and labels usually just say “Malvasia”
The revival of Vitovska: its name is clearly Slavic, and historically it was grown only in the Carso area of Trieste province and in Slovenia; it almost disappeared in the 20th century and was rescued in the 1980s

Industry scale

About 57,000 acres/23,000 ha of vineyards; most wineries are small to medium family estates, with an average holding of only about 6 acres/2.5 ha; cooperatives are few and play a marginal role — a sharp contrast with regions such as Emilia-Romagna that rely heavily on cooperatives
slides.9.title: 🍊 Orange Wine
slides.9.content:
🧡 Collio’s other philosophy

Inspired by Collio’s controversial producers Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon, one school makes white wine with red-wine techniques: long skin-contact fermentation and long ageing in large neutral oak; Gravner also introduced ancient vessels such as amphorae (anfora).

🔄 How orange wine is made

1

White grapes are crushed and fermented on their skins

→
2

Long skin contact
extracts phenolics

→
3

Long ageing in large neutral oak
or amphorae

→
4

Deep gold colour
with oxidative notes

🍷 Orange wine character

  • Colour: deep gold to amber
  • Aromas: a degree of oxidative character
  • Palate: a dense phenolic (tannic) structure
  • Food: can match richer dishes

🌟 Leading producers (Oslavia, Collio)

Josko Gravner: long skin contact, and the introduction of amphorae
Stanko Radikon: long skin contact and ageing in large casks
Grape: both are known for Ribolla Gialla
slides.10.title: 🌟 The White Wine Revolution, Super-Whites and Orange Wine
slides.10.content:
📜 Three paths for Friuli white wine

🔬 Modern whites (late 1960s)

Pioneer: Mario Schiopetto of Collio, followed by Livio Felluga and others

Technology: temperature-controlled fermentation, stainless steel, refrigeration, pneumatic presses and sterile bottling to prevent any oxidation

Style: clean, fresh, aromatic and varietally distinct

Method: no malolactic fermentation, no oak

🌟 Super-whites (from the late 1970s)

Pioneer: Jermann’s Vintage Tunina, blending native and international white grapes

Type one: aromatic, bright-acid blends fermented in stainless steel

Type two: oak-fermented and oak-aged, sometimes with late-harvested grapes for depth

Labels: Collio Bianco, Friuli Colli Orientali Bianco

Status: among the most complex white wines in Italy today

🔬 Three styles compared

1️⃣ Modern whites

◆ Protected from oxidation

◆ Stainless steel, cool fermentation

◆ No malolactic and no oak

2️⃣ The spectrum

StyleMethodColourCharacter
Modern whiteStainless steel, no oxidationPale yellowAromatic, varietally distinct
Super-whiteMulti-grape blend, oak optionalGoldenComplex structure
Orange wineLong skin contact, large casks or amphoraeDeep goldOxidative, phenolic

3️⃣ Modern cellars

◆ Wineries in Collio and Friuli Colli Orientali are still regarded as among Italy’s most modern and technically advanced

4️⃣ Progress in the vineyard

◆ From the 1970s, higher planting densities

◆ Picking at optimal ripeness

5️⃣ Minimal intervention

◆ Some producers developed a philosophy built on traditional methods and minimal intervention

🌟 Key figures

🔬 Mario Schiopetto

Pioneer of modern whites

Where: Collio

Contribution: set the standards of modern Italian white winemaking in the late 1960s

Inspiration: German winemaking

🍷 Silvio Jermann

Creator of the super-whites

Wine: Vintage Tunina

When: late 1970s

Significance: raised white blends in Friuli, and all of Italy, to a new level

🏺 Josko Gravner

Orange wine and amphorae

Where: Oslavia, Collio

Method: long skin contact; introduced amphorae

Fellow traveller: Stanko Radikon

🍷 Orange vs white vs red

FeatureTraditional whiteOrange wineRed wine
GrapesWhiteWhiteRed
Skin contactNone or very shortLongYes
TanninNone or minimalNoticeableYes
ColourPale to golden yellowDeep gold, amberRed hues
BodyLight to mediumMedium to fullMedium to full
Serving temperatureCoolerA little warmer than whiteCool room temperature

🍽️ Pairing orange wine

Orange wine has both tannin and acidity, so it can match dishes that ordinary whites struggle with.

🌶️ Rich dishes

Curries, stews

🧀 Aged cheeses

Washed-rind and hard cheeses

🍖 White meats

Roast pork, roast chicken

🥘 Spiced dishes

Middle Eastern and North African food
slides.11.title: 🗺️ The Main Appellations in Depth
slides.11.content:
👑 Collio DOC in depth

Collio (Collio Goriziano) lies in Gorizia province, along the Slovenian border between the Judrio and Isonzo rivers.

⚠️ Note: well-regarded sub-areas such as Oslavia, Capriva and San Floriano del Collio are not officially recognised by the DOC rules and cannot appear on labels. After World War II the border was redrawn so that some Collio vineyards straddle two countries, but producers may still label all their fruit Collio DOC. Sunny, often terraced slopes are called “ronchi” (singular ronco); Collio’s soil is called “Flysch di Cormons”.

⭐ Oslavia

Standing: the traditional heartland of Ribolla Gialla

Known for: home of the orange-wine producers Gravner and Radikon

🍇 Capriva del Friuli

Standing: a well-regarded unofficial sub-area

Producers: Schiopetto and others

🏛️ Cormons

Standing: gives its name to Collio’s soil, “Flysch di Cormons”

Location: the south-west of Collio

🌄 San Floriano del Collio

Standing: a well-regarded unofficial sub-area

Location: the east of Collio, next to Slovenia

🏆 The wines of Collio

Collio’s styles vary: some focus on pure varietal character, others on complexity and structure:

• Varietal whites: Sauvignon, Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Pinot Grigio, Malvasia

• Collio Bianco: the zone’s top “super-white” blends

• Reds: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, as varietals or blended into Collio Rosso

• Most planted: Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon, Friulano

⭐ Friuli Colli Orientali DOC in depth

🏆 Three DOCGs promoted from within (formerly special designations of Colli Orientali)

Friuli Venezia Giulia has 4 DOCGs, 3 of them within Friuli Colli Orientali DOC; the fourth, Lison DOCG, is shared with Veneto

💎 Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit DOCG

Grapes: at least 85% Picolit and 1 year of ageing; the traditional heartland Cialla requires 100% Picolit, higher minimum alcohol and at least 2 years, and only Cialla may use riserva (at least 4 years)

Method: traditional appassimento; Picolit’s shatter gives tiny yields

History: grown since Roman times, it declined in the early 20th century, was rescued by the Perusini family and regained its fame in the late 1960s

🍯 Ramandolo DOCG

Grape: 100% Verduzzo Giallo (called Ramandolo locally)

Status: Friuli’s first DOCG, in 2001

Terroir: small terraces cut into steep south-facing slopes (some at 30%), at 250-400 m, forming an amphitheatre; poor marl soils; far to the north, it is Friuli’s coolest growing area

Harvest: entirely by hand, often into November; most producers then dry the grapes

🌟 Rosazzo DOCG

Grapes: led by Friulano, with Sauvignon, Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay and Ribolla Gialla

Style: medium to full body, floral, nutty and spicy, with ageing potential

Area: around the Abbey of Rosazzo, founded in the late 10th century

🏛️ Historic centres

Cividale del Friuli: the centre of the zone’s wine industry

Abbazia di Rosazzo: founded in the late 10th century, once a local religious and economic centre whose monks did much for viticulture and winemaking

📍 Four traditional sub-zones

Cialla: Ribolla Gialla, Verduzzo Friulano, Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso, Schioppettino | Rosazzo: Pignolo, Ribolla Gialla | Faedis: Refosco Nostrano | Prepotto: Schioppettino

🍷 Red wine potential

The warmer southern area between Buttrio, Cividale and Manzano, moderated by Adriatic breezes, is the classic heart for reds; producers increasingly favour natives that were widely planted before phylloxera:

• Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso

• Schioppettino (Prepotto)

• Tazzelenghe

• Pignolo (Rosazzo)

Red blends are labelled Friuli Colli Orientali Rosso DOC, blending native and international grapes in any proportion

💎 Other key appellations

Friuli Isonzo DOC

Location: the plain along the Isonzo south of Collio, with potential to rival the hill appellations

Divide: the north (right bank) is cooler and mainly white; the south (left bank) is nearer the coast and more influenced by sea breezes

Sub-zones: Rive Alte (the best vineyards, only for Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Merlot); Rive di Giare (flatter, more fertile land, lighter wines, only for Pinot Grigio, Malvasia Istriana, Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso and Merlot)

Grapes: whites mainly Sauvignon, Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Malvasia Istriana; reds mainly Merlot and Refosco

Carso (Carso-Kras) DOC

Location: a limestone plateau by the Slovenian border facing the Gulf of Trieste, shaped by both Italian and Slovenian culture

Landscape: vines grow beside olive trees on small terraces called “pastini”, at 200-500 m

Soils: iron-rich red sandy clay over limestone

Key grapes: the white Vitovska and the red Terrano; “Carso” or “Carso Rosso” needs at least 70% Terrano

Style: small production with a growing reputation and a distinctive mineral, savoury character

Friuli Grave DOC

Size: Friuli’s largest DOC by area and production

Soils: the sand, clay and gravel of the central plain

Character: large volumes of Pinot Grigio and Merlot

Style: easy and fresh

📊 The main appellations at a glance

AppellationLandscapeSizeSignature style
Collio DOCEastern hillsThird largestTop whites, Collio Bianco
Friuli Colli Orientali DOCEastern hillsSecond largestReds and whites, native reds
The three DOCGsWithin Colli OrientaliVery smallPicolit and Ramandolo sweet wines; Rosazzo white
Friuli IsonzoIsonzo plainMediumA promising rising zone
CarsoLimestone plateauVery smallVitovska, Terrano
Friuli GraveCentral plainLargestEasy, everyday
slides.12.title: 🏰 Leading Producers
slides.12.content:
🧡 Skin-contact whites and the Carso

🏺 Gravner

Oslavia, Collio

Owner: Josko Gravner

Philosophy: white wine made with red-wine techniques, long skin contact and amphorae

Signature: Ribolla Gialla

Standing: a controversial and hugely influential Collio producer

🍷 Radikon

Oslavia, Collio

Founder: the late Stanko Radikon, succeeded by his son Saša

Style: long skin contact and ageing in large casks

Signature: Ribolla Gialla, Oslavje (a white blend)

🌿 Damijan Podversic

Gorizia, Collio

Style: long skin-contact whites

Signature: Ribolla Gialla, Malvasia

🏺 Vodopivec

Carso

Grape: Vitovska

Vessel: amphorae

Area: the Carso limestone plateau

🌟 Leading white wine estates

Schiopetto

Capriva del Friuli, Collio

Standing: founded by Mario Schiopetto, the starting point of the modern white wine revolution

Livio Felluga

Friuli Colli Orientali

Standing: one of the early followers of the white wine revolution

Flagship: Terre Alte (a white blend)

Hallmark: its map label

Jermann

Villanova di Farra

Signature: Vintage Tunina, which launched the “super-white” concept

Venica & Venica

Dolegna del Collio, Collio

Signature: Ronco delle Mele (Sauvignon)

Vie di Romans

Mariano del Friuli, Friuli Isonzo

Standing: a benchmark producer of the Isonzo plain

🏛️ Colli Orientali producers

⭐ Miani

Buttrio, Colli Orientali

Owner: Enzo Pontoni

Known for: tiny yields and highly sought-after whites and reds

Le Vigne di Zamò

Manzano, Colli Orientali

slides.16.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.16.points.0: ✓ Friuli lies in Italy’s north-east corner where Italian, Germanic and Slavic cultures meet, and is recognised as the birthplace of modern Italian white winemaking
slides.16.points.1: ✓ White grapes make up over 70%; the most planted are Pinot Grigio (21%), Merlot (15%) and Friulano (8%)
slides.16.points.2: ✓ In the late 1960s Mario Schiopetto introduced temperature control and stainless steel to prevent oxidation; the key to success was single-varietal bottling
slides.16.points.3: ✓ Friulano (Tocai Friulano before 2007) is the same grape as Sauvignonasse; after an EU ruling, labels may no longer use “Tocai”
slides.16.points.4: ✓ The ponca (sandstone and marl) of the eastern hills underpins the top wines of Collio and Colli Orientali
slides.16.points.5: ✓ 4 DOCGs: Picolit, Ramandolo (2001, the first) and Rosazzo all lie within Colli Orientali, plus Lison, shared with Veneto
slides.16.points.6: ✓ Jermann’s Vintage Tunina launched the “super-whites”; Gravner and Radikon used long skin contact to make “orange wine”
slides.16.points.7: ✓ Carso is known for Vitovska and Terrano (Carso Rosso needs at least 70% Terrano); Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso is the traditional signature red
slides.17.title: 🧠 Friuli Knowledge Check
slides.17.questions.0.question: Which is Friuli’s finest appellation?
slides.17.questions.0.explanation: Collio’s whites are considered the finest in Friuli and among the best in Italy; by vineyard area and production it is Friuli’s third-largest DOC.
slides.17.questions.1.question: DNA research has shown Friulano (formerly Tocai Friulano) to be identical to which grape?
slides.17.questions.1.explanation: DNA research has proven Friulano to be the same variety as Sauvignonasse, native to the Gironde; it is regarded as Friuli’s “traditional” white grape and is its third most planted variety.
slides.17.questions.2.question: How is orange wine made?
slides.17.questions.2.options.1: White grapes made with red-wine techniques (skin contact)
slides.17.questions.2.explanation: Inspired by Gravner and Radikon, some producers make white wine using red-wine techniques — long skin-contact fermentation and long ageing in large neutral oak — with Gravner also introducing amphorae; the wines are deep gold, somewhat oxidative and phenolic.
slides.17.questions.3.question: What do locals call the sandstone and calcareous marl soils of Friuli’s eastern hills?
slides.17.questions.3.explanation: The sandstone and calcareous marl of the eastern hills is called ponca locally; in Collio it is known geologically as Flysch di Cormons.
slides.17.questions.4.question: Which was the first appellation in Friuli to gain DOCG status?
slides.17.questions.4.options.1: B. Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit
slides.17.questions.4.explanation: Ramandolo became Friuli’s first DOCG in 2001; it is a sweet wine made from 100% Verduzzo Giallo (called Ramandolo locally).
slides.17.questions.5.question: Who established the standards of modern Italian white winemaking in the late 1960s?
slides.17.questions.5.explanation: Mario Schiopetto of Collio, inspired by German winemaking, introduced temperature-controlled fermentation, stainless steel, refrigeration, pneumatic presses and sterile bottling to prevent any oxidation.
slides.17.questions.6.question: Which two native grapes is Carso DOC known for?
slides.17.questions.6.explanation: Carso is known for the white Vitovska and the red Terrano, both found almost nowhere else; wines labelled “Carso” or “Carso Rosso” need at least 70% Terrano.
slides.17.questions.7.question: Which statement about Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit DOCG is correct?
slides.17.questions.7.options.1: B. Only the Cialla sub-zone may use riserva
slides.17.questions.7.options.3: D. It is a dry white
slides.17.questions.7.explanation: The base wine needs at least 85% Picolit and 1 year of ageing; Cialla requires 100% Picolit and at least 2 years, and only Cialla may use riserva (at least 4 years).
slides.17.questions.8.question: Why have labels been unable to use the word “Tocai” since 2007?
slides.17.questions.8.options.0: A. The grape was proven to be Sauvignon Blanc
slides.17.questions.8.options.1: B. The EU upheld a complaint from Hungary’s Tokaji producers
slides.17.questions.8.options.2: C. Italy switched to the original grape name
slides.17.questions.8.options.3: D. To distinguish it from Veneto
slides.17.questions.8.explanation: The EU upheld a complaint from Hungary’s Tokaji producers protecting their designation of origin, so since 2007 labels say Friulano; in Veneto the grape is called Tai or Tai Bianco.
slides.17.questions.9.question: Can Collio’s Oslavia, Capriva and San Floriano del Collio appear on labels?
slides.17.questions.9.options.0: A. Yes, they are official sub-zones
slides.17.questions.9.options.1: B. No, they are not legally recognised
slides.17.questions.9.explanation: These sub-areas are well regarded, but they are not officially recognised by the DOC rules and cannot appear on labels; they are informal zones known to the trade and consumers.
